components.text: Truth of the conclusion does not by itself supply supported premises showing that belief is epistemically reasonable.
Absolute certainty and knowledge of ultimate reality are not required for reasonable, action-guiding belief.
Truth of God's existence alone is sufficient to make belief in God reasonable.
Lack of absolute certainty prevents an atheist from having any true or reasonable belief.
The decisive claim that everyone receives certain divine revelation and suppresses knowledge of God is not directly tested.
Everyone knows the Christian God through revelation and suppresses that knowledge.
The decisive demand for a valid argument with adequately supported premises rather than absolute certainty is not answered.
The demand for a reliable method distinguishing competing revelation claims is not answered by alleging secular epistemic dependence.
Fallible supported reasoning can establish reasonable belief without absolute certainty.
Testable correlations could provide a reasonable evidential route to supernatural causation.
The earlier requirement for supported premises and valid inference is not answered by describing evolved cognition as biochemical activity.
Reasonable belief rests on valid inference and supported premises rather than absolute certainty.
Unsolved hard solipsism does not entail that fallible inquiry lacks justified starting commitments or knowledge.
The physical realization of reasoning does not itself show that reason and experience are unreliable.
Failure to solve radical skepticism makes all non-theistic truth claims unjustified.
An atheist's inability to know ultimate reality eliminates all knowledge of truth.
Asserting that God grounds logic does not demonstrate either that grounding relation or the impossibility of rival accounts.
Claiming the opponent borrows truth from Christianity does not demonstrate Christianity's exclusive explanatory necessity.
Naturalistic cognition cannot account for objective logic, whereas the pro worldview can.
The con worldview must borrow truth and reasoning from Christianity.
A perfect divine source does not by itself explain how a fallible human recipient acquires infallibly accurate revelation.
Invoking revelation to certify the worldview that certifies revelation reproduces the challenged justificatory circle.
Divine revelation enables human beings to know objective truth with certainty.
Starting with God removes the con side's inability to know truth.
Human uncertainty and asserted certainty do not establish God's existence or supply a valid, evidentially supported argument.
The premise that God exists still requires support before the syllogism establishes reasonable belief.
A challenge to secular certainty does not itself demonstrate the divine account of truth or logic.
Human uncertainty entails that truth cannot be known unless inquiry begins with God.
God's asserted existence makes belief in God reasonable.
Everyone knows God exists despite contrary professions.
The demand for evidence that God exists and for a valid bridge from uncertainty to God is not answered.
The fallibilist reliance on generally reliable shared experience is rejected but not shown to be insufficient.
The demand to demonstrate divine grounding and Christian exclusivity remains unanswered.
Generally reliable experience and reason can ground fallible inquiry without adding God.
Reality rather than asserted certainty is the arbiter of truth.
The requested mechanism connecting a perfect divine source to certain knowledge in a fallible recipient is not supplied.
The demand for a reliable method distinguishing competing revelation claims is not answered.
The demand for evidence supporting God's existence is answered only by saying evidence already presupposes God.
A mechanism must connect a perfect divine source to infallible knowledge in a fallible recipient.
Evidence can warrant supernatural belief through reliable, testable correlation.
The demand for certainty through God is rejected because rational prediction can be justified probabilistically rather than infallibly.
The broader claim that fallibility eliminates knowledge is answered by distinguishing rational justification from certainty.
Evidence and rational inference are intelligible only if one first presupposes God.
Non-theistic reasoning cannot justify truth claims from experience.
Using past regularity to justify future-oriented induction employs the very inductive method whose validity is under challenge.
Past recurring success provides probabilistic justification for expecting future regularity.
The repeated claim that naturalism cannot account for logical absolutes does not establish that Christianity can do so.
Defining truth by God's mind does not demonstrate the divine grounding relation.
Appealing to revelation does not answer the exclusive-accounting demand.
A difficulty for secular induction does not independently establish Christianity's explanatory success.
Only the theistic worldview can account for logical absolutes and objective truth.
Truth must conform to an absolute divine mind to be knowable.
Evidence and truth presuppose God.
The request for a positive account of logical absolutes is answered by saying they reflect God's thinking and are known by revelation.
The demand to demonstrate the grounding relation and exclude rival accounts remains unanswered.
The requested mechanism for reliable human revelation remains unanswered.
The pro side must demonstrate how God accounts for logic and why that account is exclusive.
Attributing logical absolutes to God is insufficient without demonstrating adequacy and exclusivity.
The rival-revelation challenge is contacted through an internal-consistency test comparing Quranic claims about the Bible with conflict between the texts.
The human transmission and certainty mechanism for revelation is not answered.
Competing revelations lack a reliable method for distinguishing which religious authority is true.
Revelation requires a demonstrated truth-preserving mechanism for fallible recipients.
The demand for an inference from shared logical absolutes to God is replaced by a precondition claim because the argument is transcendental rather than deductive.
The demand to demonstrate that Christianity uniquely supplies the alleged precondition remains unanswered.
The probabilistic defense of induction is not directly answered by clarifying the argument's direction.
Recurring experience probabilistically justifies inductive expectations without deductive certainty.
Christianity's exclusive explanatory ability requires demonstration rather than assertion.
Installing Christianity as a necessary starting point does not demonstrate its truth, necessity, or reasonableness.
The factual premise that God exists remains unsupported.
Asserted certainty about God's perspective does not establish objective truth or human access to it.
Saying logic reflects God's thinking does not demonstrate the grounding relation.
Criticizing one rival revelation does not establish Christianity's reliability.
Challenging secular induction does not shift the positive burden of demonstrating Christian necessity.
Christianity may be installed as the necessary precondition for all absolutes rather than inferred from them.
Logical absolutes are accounted for by God's thinking and revelation.
Secular induction is viciously circular.
Belief in God is reasonable because the proposition is true.
